newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OPINION - S.African budget fudging - By E.Osborn.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - S.African budget fudging - By E.Osborn.

text.p: By Edward Osborn, economic consultant to Edey Rogers & Co Ltd

The conviction with which the Minister of Finance holds to his claim of getting the budget deficit down to 4.0 percent of GDP next fiscal year, 1997/98, despite a number of possibly adversely militating factors, arouses suspicions that he has fall-back plans to achieve this creatively, if necessary.
The budget plan leak last November has prepared the ground for a general public expectation that this is achievable in the normal straightforward way of budget discipline and frugality.
According to that leak, blazoned conveniently in a leading Sunday newspaper, expenditure planning was to be limited to 185.5 billion rand, or a mere 6.8 percent growth on that budgeted for 1996/97.

After allowing for the likely substantial growth of the interest bill because of high interest rates this past year, the implied growth of non-interest expenditures will be of the order of 4.9 percent, which is negative growth in real terms of the order of four percent -- a most unlikely budgetary parameter.
Significantly no formal government announcement was made; the leak came in the form of a copy of Cabinet Minutes, marked Top Secret.

This, of course, raises serious questions about the security of Cabinet Minutes and, in particular, Minutes dealing with budgetary matters. Finance Ministers have lost their heads for less in other countries.

That peccadillo apart, the leak must have been inspired by thoughts of impressing the world of government's renewed determination to achieve fiscal virtue. It was certainly swallowed rapturously by a breathless financial editor.

There was a no pause on his part to consider that budgetary planning always starts with a Cabinet paper from a Minister of Finance that outlines the desired parameters of the budget couched in the severest terms. What finally emerges in the budget is the outcome of months of haggling and in-fighting in estimates committees.

Nevertheless the Minister of Finance has plenty of scope to achieve his goals through creative forecasting of revenues but there is a limit to that route in that his reputation will ultimately be tarnished, unless he knows that he is not going to be around for much longer. The best alternatives for budgetary fudging lie in manipulations which are not overt.

In Europe with the imminent need to comply with the Maastricht criterion of a percent deficit for membership of the common currency union, budgetary fudging plans have reached a new height in inventiveness and cynicism.
A few examples:
- Italy's Eurotax, an ad hoc tax, which is really a loan in that it will be rebated against future taxes
- Germany's creative forecasting and deliberate underestimate of unemployment costs
- France's one-off cash payment by France Telecom to the French Treasury in exchange for the future pension liabilities of the company.

But, of course, of direct import for South Africa, there is also the possibility of European central bank disposal of gold reserves, the proceeds of which would be transferred to the respective country treasuries. This threat itself is currently having a direful depressing effect on the gold price.

There must be considerable scope for fudging the accounts in South Africa not immediately obvious to an outsider, but three stand out as possibilities in respect of state pension funds, the interest bill and foreign debt redemption.

As far as the pension funds are concerned there are government contributions in addition to employee contributions in the ratio of 2.8 to one. The surplus funds of the pension funds are mostly invested in government stock. Government's contributions are of the order of five billion rand per annum. A considerable cash-flow saving could be effected by temporarily dropping the employer ratio to something lower, say 0.8, as Minister Chris Liebenberg did in 1994 in order to finance salary increases.

A convenient alternative is to drop the state contribution altogether and simply replace it by the issue of government notes. Government's actuarial obligations would still be honoured. The current benefit payments and expenditure of the funds are more than adequately covered by current earnings of the funds in the form of interest and dividends on the funds' assets.
A saving of five billion rand would automatically reduce the deficit and, indeed, on this year's budget would have reduced it from 5.1 percent to 4.2 percent.

The second possibility that comes to mind is that of reversing or suspending the practice of including an imputed interest in the interest bill in respect of zero-coupon stocks. This could be justified on the grounds that no cash flow is involved and that the deficit to be funded by borrowing should be reduced accordingly.

Zero-coupon stocks other than those in respect of forex losses currently amount to some 3.3 billion rand and the imputed interest would be of the order of 200 million rand. With these out of the way there would be a further marginal reduction of the deficit.
Associated with this would be the deferment until times are more propitious of plans to make entries for the amortisation of discounts on stock issued.

However, of greater significance could be a change in the treatment of accounting for the redemption of foreign debt. At present the forex loss on debt redeemed is included under the dubious title of "management costs" with the service costs of debt, with the original book value of the debt being stated as the amount of debt to be redeemed. The forex losses thus enter into the deficit. An alternative treatment would be to show the estimated foreign debt to be redeemed in rand terms thus eliminating the service cost.

In 1996/97 these forex costs were estimated to be 858 million rand -- but will turn out to be closer to 1.2 billion. In this coming year the only relevant debt for redemption or roll-over is the $750 million IMF loan which could bear a forex loss, or management cost of 1.0 billion rand, or nearly 0.2 percnet of GDP.

All these changes or deferment of plans amount to putting the budget more strictly onto a cash flow basis and there is, arguably, virtue in that, but the move would achieve a much lower deficit ratio instantaneously and the Minister could emerge as a hero in his time without anyone really understanding why.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters.)
10 January 1997
